newsitem.title: INDIA: India farmers clash with gov't over wheat prices.
newsitem.headline: India farmers clash with gov't over wheat prices.

text.p: Farmers in agriculturally-rich northern Indian states have clashed with the government over wheat purchase prices threatening procurement operations amid falling stocks, trade and state officials said on Tuesday.
Indian government ministers early this month agreed to pay a bonus of 600 rupees ($16.70) per tonne to farmers in addition to the current purchase price of 4,150 rupees.
The bonus will be payable on wheat offered for sale to procurement agencies for the central pool up to June 10, 1997.

Farmers in the states of Punjab and Haryana, which contribute 80 percent of the country's wheat output, have been agitating for higher prices, seeking parity with the prices at which the government imports wheat.

"The minimum price acceptable to us is 715 rupees per quintal (100 kgs), though we are demanding 785 rupees," Balbir Singh Rajewal, secretary of the Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU), a farmers' organisation, told Reuters in the northern city of Chandigarh.
BKU president Bhupinder Singh Mann said that though the government was importing wheat at $180 per tonne, it was not even giving minimum prices to the farmers.
"It is discrimination. Are we trying to kill the farm sector?" Mann asked.

But Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra on Monday ruled out any further increase in the bonus to farmers and warned that the government might be forced to import additional wheat if farmers refuse to sell their produce to official agencies.
"I cannot let the people starve," newspapers quoted Mishra as saying. He ruled out paying the prices at which India imports wheat.

India's state-run State Trading Corporation said last week it had contracted to import 2.74 million tonnes of wheat since December 1996, when the government authorised imports to build stocks and check prices.
The Agriculture Ministry has put the 1996/97 (July-June) wheat crop at 64.5 million tonnes against 62.6 million in 1995/96.
Farmers have the backing of Chief Minister Prakash Singh Badal, who heads Punjab and Chief Minister Bansi Lal, who heads Haryana, in their demand for higher prices.

"It will be better if the government revises the procurement price and fixes it at 550 rupees per quintal (5,500 ruppees/tonne)," Badal said. "Only then we will be able to achieve the procurement target."

Officials of the state-run Food Corporation of India (FCI), India's largest grain procurement agency, said it had so far not procured any wheat from the two states since arrivals normally start only in mid-April.
The government had announced it would advance wheat procurement from March 17, as against the first week of April to augment domestic supplies and check rising prices.

Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told parliament in March that India's wheat stocks on April 1 were projected at 2.72 million tonnes, down one million from the buffer stock norms of 3.7 million tonnes set by the government.

Punjab and Haryana together annually contribute about nine million tonnes of wheat to the central pool, roughly 80 percent of the total procurement. Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh are the other major wheat-producing states.
